issue: The caption calls all five 'selection surfaces' model-selection dimensions, but one surface, 'retrieve-vs-generate', is an architecture decision rather than a model-selection dimension.
evidence: Figure's 'Five selection surfaces' box lists 'quality · latency · KV cache · $/tok · retrieve-vs-generate'. Caption: 'The five surfaces are the model-selection dimensions.' The diagram then splits into 'Retrieval leg' and 'Generation leg', which is a system-architecture decision.
acceptance_test: Either remove 'retrieve-vs-generate' from the five model-selection surfaces and show it as a separate architecture decision, or reword the caption to distinguish four model-selection dimensions from the retrieve-vs-generate architecture choice.

issue: The figure introduces a second, competing taxonomy that contradicts the one established one chapter earlier, and the relationship between the two is never stated. FIG 4.1 (PDF 93 / printed 73) presents 'the six workload dimensions' (Quality requirements; Traffic/concurrency; Token profile; Latency SLO; Economic constraints; Operational constraints) as the book's workload-characterization vocabulary. FIG 5.1's top box, also labelled 'Workload characterization', lists only three items: 'tokens · cost · SLO'. A reader who has just absorbed the six-dimension frame will read the three-item box as a contradiction (or, worse, as a silent narrowing of the framework). Separately, the caption calls the five boxes 'the model-selection dimensions', introducing a third label for what are visibly derived from the Chapter 4 dimensions (latency -> Latency SLO; KV cache -> Token profile; S/Tok -> Economic constraints). The book never says whether the five surfaces are a subset of the six dimensions, a refinement of them, or an orthogonal axis.
evidence: Page 73 figure header 'WORKLOAD DIMENSION' with six rows; caption: 'The six workload dimensions and the architectural decision each one drives'. Page 92 figure box 1: 'Workload characterization' / 'tokens · cost · SLO'; caption: 'The five surfaces are the model-selection dimensions'. No cross-reference to Chapter 4 or to FIG 4.1 appears on page 92.
acceptance_test: Either (a) relabel the top box 'Workload characterization (subset shown: tokens · cost · SLO)' and add a caption clause stating that only the dimensions that bind model selection are drawn, or (b) replace the three items with the Chapter 4 vocabulary. In addition, add one caption sentence defining the relation between the six workload dimensions and the five selection surfaces (e.g. 'the five surfaces are the subset of the six dimensions that constrain model choice; the remaining dimension, Operational constraints, is out of scope for this figure'). Verify that a reader who has read p. 73 can state whether the five surfaces are a subset, a refinement, or a separate axis.

issue: The abbreviation 'S/Tok' in the 'Five selection surfaces' box is undefined on the page and has two plausible readings that are not equivalent, one of which duplicates an adjacent term. Reading A: 'seconds per token' (i.e. TPOT / decode latency), which duplicates the adjacent surface 'latency'. Reading B: '$ per token' (cost per token), which duplicates the 'cost' item in the box immediately above ('tokens · cost · SLO'). Because the figure is the reader's first encounter with the token, and because the caption's whole argument is that the five surfaces are a distinct set, an ambiguous member of that set weakens the figure's central claim. The book elsewhere uses 'TPOT' for time-per-output-token, so a reader is likely to reach for that reading and then find the surface list redundant.
evidence: Figure box 2 sub-label: 'quality · latency · KV cache · S/Tok · retrieve-vs-generate'. Figure box 1 sub-label: 'tokens · cost · SLO'. Caption: 'The five surfaces are the model-selection dimensions'. No expansion of 'S/Tok' appears in the caption, the figure, or the visible page text.
acceptance_test: Replace 'S/Tok' with an unambiguous phrase ('cost per token' or 'seconds per output token'), or define the abbreviation in the caption and in the glossary. Confirm that the resulting five-item list contains no item that restates 'latency' or 'cost' from the box above. Verify against the Chapter 5 body text that the chosen expansion matches the term the chapter actually uses.

issue: The word 'quality' denotes two different things inside one figure, and the caption asserts they are distinct without disambiguating them. 'quality' is one of the five selection surfaces in the drawn box; 'retrieval quality' and 'final answer quality' are two of the five end-to-end evaluation gates listed in the caption. The caption's claim that the surfaces are 'deliberately distinct from the end-to-end evaluation gates' is therefore made using an identical word for one surface and two gates, with no clause saying which 'quality' the surface refers to. A reader can plausibly conclude that the 'quality' surface IS the retrieval-quality gate, which is precisely the confusion the caption says it is excluding.
evidence: Figure box 2 sub-label: 'quality · latency · KV cache · S/Tok · retrieve-vs-generate'. Caption: 'they are deliberately distinct from the end-to-end evaluation gates (retrieval quality, reranking, embedding recall, grounding, and final answer quality) that a RAG system must also pass'.
acceptance_test: Rename the surface so it cannot collide with a gate name (e.g. 'answer-quality bar' or 'quality requirement'), and/or add a caption clause naming which quality each refers to. Verify that no reader can map the surface 'quality' onto either 'retrieval quality' or 'final answer quality' without re-reading the caption.

issue: The drawing implies that all five selection surfaces apply to both legs, but the surfaces are not leg-symmetric. A single 'Five selection surfaces' box fans out through two arrows labelled 'split' to 'Retrieval leg' and 'Generation leg', which reads as 'these five surfaces are then evaluated for each leg'. Two of the five are generation-leg concepts: an embedding model has no autoregressive KV cache, and it has no per-token decode cost of the kind 'S/Tok' denotes. The figure therefore permits the inference that the embedding model has a KV cache, which is a substantive architectural error rather than a stylistic one.
evidence: Figure: 'Five selection surfaces' -> two arrows labelled 'split' -> 'Retrieval leg' (embedding · 768-dim) and 'Generation leg' (70B FP16 · serving). Surface list includes 'KV cache' and 'S/Tok'. Caption describes the surfaces as applying to 'model selection' generally and does not qualify which surfaces bind which leg.
acceptance_test: Annotate the two split arrows with the surfaces that bind each leg (e.g. 'quality · latency · cost/token' for retrieval; 'quality · latency · KV cache · cost/token' for generation), or add a caption sentence stating that the surfaces are evaluated per leg and that KV cache and per-token decode cost apply only to the generation leg. Verify that no reader concludes the embedding model holds a KV cache.

issue: The caption's parenthetical is missing a separator and reads as a run-on: 'two legs (retrieval/embedding generation/70B)'. The intended reading is '(retrieval/embedding, generation/70B)', matching the drawn boxes 'Retrieval leg - embedding · 768-dim' and 'Generation leg - 70B FP16 · serving'. As printed, 'embedding generation' can be parsed as a single phrase, which is confusing in a figure whose whole point is that the two legs are distinct.
evidence: Caption: 'Model selection for RAG workload - five selection surfaces -> two legs (retrieval/embedding generation/70B) -> the system decision.'
acceptance_test: Render as 'two legs (retrieval/embedding, generation/70B)'. Verify the parenthetical maps one-to-one onto the two drawn leg boxes.

issue: The 'Generation leg' box is drawn with a visibly heavier and darker border than every other box in the figure (including its sibling 'Retrieval leg'). The emphasis is unexplained by the caption or the prose. It matters more than a cosmetic inconsistency because, in grayscale, all five box fills fall in a narrow light band (green, pink, purple, tan, blue-gray all convert to roughly 78-82% gray), so the border weight is the only visual differentiator between the two legs once color is removed. An unexplained emphasis cue that survives grayscale is a semantic claim the reader cannot decode.
evidence: Rendered page 92: 'Generation leg' box outline is thicker and darker than 'Retrieval leg', 'Workload characterization', 'Five selection surfaces', and 'RAG system decision'. No caption clause refers to emphasis, the canonical model, or the 70B leg being the subject of the chapter.
acceptance_test: Normalize all five box borders to the same weight and color, or state the reason for the emphasis in the caption (e.g. 'the generation leg is the subject of this chapter'). Verify that in a grayscale rendering the two legs are distinguished by their labels and by nothing else.

issue: The five selection surfaces are drawn as a single run-on line of dot-separated words ('quality · latency · KV cache · S/Tok · retrieve-vs-generate'), which renders them as an undifferentiated list. The caption's argument depends on the reader being able to count and individuate the five surfaces and hold them apart from the five evaluation gates, but the drawing provides no visual structure that supports that count. Five discrete chips (or a two-column mini-list) would make the 'five' verifiable at a glance and would also make the leg-specific applicability (see FIG-5.1-03) expressible.
evidence: Figure box 2 sub-label is one continuous line of five items; caption: 'The five surfaces are the model-selection dimensions; they are deliberately distinct from the end-to-end evaluation gates'.
acceptance_test: Render the five surfaces as five visually discrete items. Verify that a reader can count five without reading the caption, and that the count matches the caption's enumeration.

issue: The diagram's structure reads as two parallel legs converging on a decision, with no depiction of the retrieved context entering the generation leg. The 'context' arrow runs from 'Retrieval leg' directly to 'RAG system decision', bypassing 'Generation leg'. The caption frames the figure as a selection map rather than a pipeline, which makes the parallel reading defensible, but the drawing alone permits the inference that the two legs are independent selections whose outputs are combined only at the end - i.e. that the retrieved context is not an input to generation. That is the defining structural property of RAG and the figure is the natural place a reader would look for it.
evidence: Figure: arrow labelled 'context' from 'Retrieval leg' to 'RAG system decision'; arrow labelled 'answer' from 'Generation leg' to 'RAG system decision'; no arrow from 'Retrieval leg' to 'Generation leg'. Caption: '...this figure is a selection map, not an evaluation pipeline.'
acceptance_test: Either route the 'context' arrow into the 'Generation leg' box (with 'answer' continuing to the system decision), or add a caption clause: 'the two legs are selected in parallel; the retrieved context is supplied to the generation leg at serving time (not shown)'. Verify that no reader concludes the legs are independent of one another.

figure: Figure 6.1 (metric hierarchy as a diagnostic chain)
issue: Queue depth is classified as a Resource metric in Figure 6.1 but as a Serving metric in the immediately preceding prose, and the figure's Resource box also silently drops 'memory pressure', which the prose lists as the fourth resource metric.
evidence: Prose, PDF 114 / printed 94, item 2: 'Serving metrics — ... Time-to-first-token (TTFT), time-per-output-token (TPOT), inter-token latency, queue depth (a scheduler state), and goodput'; item 3: 'Resource metrics — ... HBM bandwidth utilization, FLOP utilization / model FLOPs utilization (MFU), KV cache occupancy, and memory pressure.' Figure 6.1 boxes read 'Resource metrics: HBM BW · MFU · KV occupancy · queue depth' and 'Serving metrics: TTFT · TPOT · goodput'. The figure is the chapter's canonical three-layer mental model, so a metric appearing in the wrong layer directly contradicts the taxonomy the prose defines (queue depth is explicitly parenthesized as 'a scheduler state', i.e. serving-layer, in the prose).
acceptance_test: The figure's Resource box lists exactly the prose's four resource metrics (HBM BW, MFU, KV occupancy, memory pressure) and queue depth appears either in the Serving box or is explicitly justified as a resource-layer item in both prose and figure with identical wording; re-render PDF 115 and confirm box contents match PDF 114 items 2–3.

issue: The figure classifies 'queue depth' as a Resource metric, while the preceding page explicitly classifies it as a Serving metric (a scheduler state).
evidence: Page 94 text: 'Serving metrics — ... Time-to-first-token (TTFT), time-per-output-token (TPOT), inter-token latency, queue depth (a scheduler state), and goodput...' Figure 6.1's 'Resource metrics' box lists 'HBM BW · MFU · KV occupancy · queue depth'. This is a direct contradiction in the book's three-layer metric taxonomy.
acceptance_test: Move 'queue depth' to the Serving metrics box in Fig 6.1, or reclassify it consistently in the p94 text and explain why it is a resource metric; ensure the three-layer taxonomy matches.

issue: The figure's three-layer metric taxonomy contradicts the prose on the preceding page (printed p.94, §6.1). The figure places 'queue depth' in the Resource metrics box and omits 'memory pressure', whereas the prose lists queue depth under Serving metrics ('a scheduler state') and lists memory pressure under Resource metrics. The prose explicitly states that Fig 6.1 is how the three layers are stacked, so the figure must reproduce the prose's grouping; as drawn it does not.
evidence: Figure Resource box: 'HBM BW · MFU · KV occupancy · queue depth'; figure Serving box: 'TTFT · TPOT · goodput'. Prose p.94 Serving metrics: '... inter-token latency, queue depth (a scheduler state), and goodput'; prose p.94 Resource metrics: 'HBM bandwidth utilization, FLOP utilization / model FLOPs utilization (MFU), KV cache occupancy, and memory pressure.'
acceptance_test: Move 'queue depth' out of the Resource box (into the Serving box, or mark it as a scheduler-state item on the serving side) and add 'memory pressure' to the Resource box so the figure's boxes match the prose's serving/resource lists; or, if the figure is intentionally an abbreviated/alternative grouping, add a caption sentence stating the figure shows representative metrics and that queue depth is treated as a serving/scheduler state in §6.1. Re-render and confirm no metric sits in a different layer than in the prose.
